one_liner: AES-based backtracking-resistant PRNG (C++11 URBG) at roughly std::mt19937_64 speed; reference code for absl::BitGen's engine.
what_it_does: Randen is a 'strong' pseudorandom generator: outputs are indistinguishable from random and leaking the current state does not reveal earlier outputs. randen::Randen<T> (T = any built-in unsigned type) implements the C++11 UniformRandomBitGenerator interface (seed, discard, stream operators, reseed from a SeedSequence), so it plugs into std:: distributions and std::shuffle in place of std::mt19937_64. The repo is a research reference implementation (randen.h/.cc plus vector128.h and benchmarks); the maintained production version is Abseil's absl::random (absl::BitGen).
how_it_is_fast: It plugs a 2048-bit Simpira-v2-style permutation (a 16-branch generalized Feistel network with improved block shuffle, 17 rounds of 2-round AES-128 functions) into the Reverie sponge construction, so one permutation call refills a 240-byte output buffer while keeping a 128-bit hidden capacity for backtracking resistance. The AES rounds run on hardware AES instructions (AES-NI, POWER8 VSX crypto, ARMv8 crypto), and operator() is just a buffer read with a rare refill branch.
when_to_use: You want a default generator that is safe if outputs or state might be attacker-observable (shuffles, sampling, randomized algorithms in services) without paying CTR-DRBG or /dev/urandom costs (~10x slower in the README table).

Applied workloads (shuffle, reservoir sampling, Monte Carlo) on x86 with AES-NI where std::mt19937_64 is the incumbent: about 1.1x faster geomean per the paper, with 256 bytes of state versus mt19937_64's ~2.5 KB.
Already on Abseil: use absl::BitGen, which is this algorithm with runtime AES dispatch and a portable fallback.
x86-64 with AES-NI, POWER8+ with VSX, or ARMv8 with crypto extensions.
when_not_to_use: Raw throughput is the goal: pcg64_c32 is ~2x faster in the tight-loop microbenchmark (0.78 vs 1.54 cpb) and the paper's shuffle tables show PCG ahead; non-crypto generators like Romu or xoshiro are faster still.
Targets without hardware AES: the standalone repo has no software fallback (vector128.h hits #error "Port"); only Abseil ships a slow portable path.
You need a vetted CSPRNG for keys/tokens: the README says the algorithm is 'still under review and subject to change' and the paper is not peer reviewed.
You need a maintained standalone library: archived 2023-06-12, last commit 2018-10-05, no versioned releases or build system beyond a Makefile.
Performance depends heavily on compiler unrolling: README reports up to 1.6x more cycles/byte with GCC 7.3 and 1.3x with Clang 4.0.1.

integration.min_toolchain: C++11; Makefile uses clang++ -O3 -mavx2 -maes; Clang recommended for loop unrolling
integration.platforms: x86 with SSE2+AES-NI, POWER8 with VSX, ARMv8 with NEON+crypto; build fails elsewhere
integration.thread_safety: not documented; engine is a plain mutable object with no synchronization (Abseil states its BitGen is not thread safe, like std engines)

gotchas: Must be compiled with AES enabled (-maes or equivalent); there is no runtime CPU dispatch in this repo.
Object is alignas(32) with 256 bytes of state; heap allocation of the engine relies on aligned new (C++17) or a custom allocator under C++11.
Backtracking resistance only covers outputs before the last Generate call; prediction resistance needs periodic reseed() with fresh entropy.
Output stream may change if the algorithm is revised (README: 'subject to change'); Abseil's absl::BitGen deliberately offers no seed stability across runs.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Randen when you need attack resistance (indistinguishability plus backtracking resistance) at near-Mersenne-Twister cost; Romu, SIMDxorshift and Randompack are faster but non-cryptographic, and Squares/Philox-style counter-based RNGs suit parallel stream splitting rather than state-compromise resistance.
verified_claims_summary: On an Intel Xeon E5-2690 v3 (Haswell) with Clang -O3, Google's paper reports Randen about 1.1x faster than std::mt19937_64 (geomean over shuffle, reservoir sampling and Monte Carlo, also on POWER8), while pcg64_c32 is fastest on x86; the README's tight-loop microbenchmark shows 1.54 cpb vs 1.79 for mt19937_64 and 0.78 for pcg64_c32. The standard library implementation for mt19937_64 is not named.
status_note: Archived since 2023-06-12 (last commit 2018-10-05) but Apache-2.0 and small enough to vendor; for production prefer the maintained Abseil absl::BitGen implementation.
